newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Climate cuts Morocco's productive farmland 21 pct.
newsitem.headline: Climate cuts Morocco's productive farmland 21 pct.

text.p: Morocco's productive farmland fell by 21 percent to 4.5 million hectares in the 1996/97 season from the previous season because of weather changes, the official MAP news agency said on Thursday.

MAP quoted Agriculture Minister Hassan Abou Ayoub as saying "Morocco's cultivated areas were reduced by more than 21 percent to 4.5 million hectares in 1996/1997 from 5.7 million hectares in the 1995/96 agricultural season."
This was due to "climate changes which caused local disasters in some regions of the kingdom," MAP quoted Ayoub as telling a parliamentary session.

Among areas hit by heavy winter rains was the southern region of Haouz which had 35,000 hectares cultivated with cereals, sugarbeet, potatoes and fruit, the agency said. No details of other damaged agricultural areas mentioned by the minister, such as the eastern province of Oujda, were immediately available.
According to Ayoub, the government, which is due to present a draft budget before parliament soon, will take action over the climate's impact on farmers in the 1997/98 state budget.
The finance ministry earlier said it expects Gross Domestic Product to show negative growth of minus 1.0 percent in 1997 due a drop in agricultural output.
The state budget will be effective from July 1, 1997 but must be adopted by the 333-seat parliament before end of June, the ministry added.

The Casablanca-based think-tank Centre Marocain de Conjoncture also said Morocco's economy "may stagnate or drop to minus one percent in 1997 from 11.8 percent growth in 1996, due mainly to the declining trend of agricultural output."
Agriculture represents nearly 20 percent of Morocco's GDP and employs 50 percent of its estimated 10 million workforce.
Morocco harvested 10 million tonnes of cereals in 1995/96 against 1.6 million tonnes in 1994/95 when it was hit by what the authorities called "the drought of the century".

The government, which expected the country's GDP to grow at between 3.5 and 4.0 percent this year based on a modest cereals harvest of 7.0 million tonnes, has revised its forecast downward, the finance ministry said.
